April 30, 1952 is recorded as the end date on the inclusive reading (the exemption runs through that day); the exclusive reading, under which it ends as April 30 begins, is the alternative. No held order revokes or extends the exemption, so this is the first end. State on 2026-10-14: terminated.

EO 10229 (16 FR 2865, Federal Register of Tuesday, April 3, 1951; signed March 30, 1951; F.R. Doc. 51-4006) has one operative command: under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 404; 5 U.S.C. 715a) the President exempts Hugh H. Bennett, Chief of the Soil Conservation Service, from compulsory retirement for age under the Civil Service Retirement Act of May 29, 1930, for a stated period. The order fixes its own term, so the first end is the own-terms end date April 30, 1952. Under the 2026-10-21 until-date ruling it is recorded inclusive (the exemption runs through the end of April 30, 1952); the exclusive reading, under which the term ends as April 30 begins, is the alternative. The held Federal Register text confirms identity (number, title, date and document number agree with the census register row). The end is cited to the held Federal Register text of the order itself, a government printed copy (OCR text layer of the official PDF, whose page images were not opened), because the packet registers no own-term record on that text.

research_rationale:
EO 10295 (16 FR 10011; signed September 28, 1951) approves a seal of office for the United States Court of Military Appeals: "I hereby approve such seal as the official seal of the United States Court of Military Appeals." The preceding recital describes the design and says the design "accompanies and is hereby made a part of this order". The command is a one-time approval that was complete when the President signed the order; the text has no delayed-effect wording. Under the 2026-10-28 evidence ruling the command is exhausted by performance on September 28, 1951, and the surviving consequence (that the approved design is the Court's official seal) is separated and recorded in savings rather than treated as a command of this order that continues. The dossier's machine own-term leads for this number come from the Court's later rules of practice, which are not this order's terms and are not used.

EO 10388 (17 FR 7877; signed August 27, 1952; F.R. Doc. 52-9589) revokes Executive Order No. 8616 of December 19, 1940, which placed Palmyra Island under the control and jurisdiction of the Secretary of the Navy and reserved it for naval purposes: "Executive Order No. 8616 ... is hereby revoked." The command is a one-time act that took effect when the President signed it; it contains no delayed-effect wording, and the held Federal Register page prints it as signed August 27, 1952. Under the 2026-10-28 evidence ruling, the command is exhausted by performance on that date and the surviving consequence, that Executive Order No. 8616 no longer governs, is separated from the exhausted command and recorded in savings. The held text of Executive Order No. 8616 is an earlier instrument that this order revokes; it is not a later event.

research_rationale:
EO 10417A (17 FR 11187; signed December 6, 1952) closes the executive departments, independent establishments and other agencies in the District of Columbia metropolitan area "all day on Friday, December 26, 1952, the day following Christmas Day," and excuses employees in the metropolitan area and the field service from duty on that day, except those whom agency heads exclude for special public reasons or whose absence would be inconsistent with law. The letter suffix is part of the order number. The command applies to one named day, so it ends with December 26, 1952 by its own terms; the order names the whole day, so the end is the close of that day and the exclusive reading does not arise. The end source is the held Federal Register text of the order itself, which has no separately registered own-term record.

liens on real estate ) for borrowers re­
ceiving loans under Commodity Credit

ity loan is less than the market value of
